description: De-identified evidence-only derivative for research review and later AI use. Original documents are not included.
limitations: Selective extraction of three coded themes per document. Nuance, direct quotations and contextual detail have been reduced to minimise identification risk. Not a full anonymised transcript corpus. Residual recognition from research themes cannot be ruled out.
use_rules: Use evidence IDs when referring to a coded theme.
These are selective paraphrases of analytical summaries, not quotations, transcripts or validated generalisations.
Do not infer participant names, employers, locations, job histories or specific managerial roles.
Do not map a source automatically to CEO, sustainability manager or operational manager. Role-specific applications must be labelled as model inferences.
Do not treat repetition of a theme as a prevalence estimate or statistical prediction.
Do not classify a candidate as an integrated KPI solely because it appears in the catalogue. Check that it connects financial and sustainability dimensions.
Do not infer a formula where none is specified.
Do not reuse legacy workbook classifications without reconciling them with the current framework.
Evidence can support, qualify or challenge an assessment; return insufficient evidence where necessary.

Incomplete operating data can obstruct otherwise straightforward calculations.
A shared method may help functions discuss financial and environmental trade-offs.

Integrated indicators may complement separate measures rather than replace them.
Metric design needs a connection to strategy and resource allocation.

Relative measures may obscure absolute outcomes that remain unacceptable.

Disclosure of new information may introduce reputational concerns.
Links to remuneration can influence whether sustainability considerations affect behaviour.
Short decision horizons can conflict with longer-term sustainability outcomes.
Stable measurement methods can support confidence in comparisons over time.
Intensity indicators require checking whether movements in the denominator change the interpretation of performance.
External comparison can favour consistent methods over customised construction.
Leadership changes may weaken the continuity of sustainability targets.
A material relationship with financial performance can provide a starting point for design.
Trust in a measure and usefulness for decisions should be examined separately.
External reporting adoption may depend on whether intended users actually use the metric.
Consistent base-data definitions and calculation methods can support derived indicators.
Performance incentives can create unintended behaviours that undermine the intended outcome.
Integrated measures may be embedded within existing accounting processes.
Activity associated with transition investments can increase measured emissions, complicating interpretation.
A metric useful for comparing investments may not suit individual project selection.
Investment mandates and return requirements can constrain adoption of sustainability measures.
Integrated measures may be easier to sustain when embedded in existing management systems.
Duplicate reporting processes can increase implementation burdens.
A measure that is material in one activity may have little relevance in another.
Costs relative to emissions reductions can support prioritisation of decarbonisation measures.
Environmental impact relative to expenditure can support internal budget discussions.
Links between financing terms and sustainability performance may provide a route to adoption.
Reporting requirements can consume capacity that might otherwise support implementation.
Peer adoption and perceived risk may influence interest in voluntary metrics.
Disclosure obligations and performance improvement are distinct motivations.
Stakeholder demand for comparability can motivate voluntary measurement.
Annual reporting frequency may be inadequate for decisions requiring more frequent information.
Information systems and staff capability can constrain implementation.
Combining uncertain sustainability data with financial data does not remove uncertainty.
Facility-level analysis may be more actionable than company-level aggregation.
A relationship between component variables should be established before integration.
Missing value-chain emissions data can prevent meaningful integrated measurement.
The marginal effort of combining existing data may be modest, while collecting missing data can be substantial.
Customer demands can motivate measurement even without direct reporting obligations.
Combining variables can reduce interpretability even when integration is intended to help.
A coordinated set of separate measures may be preferable to one combined indicator.
Expenditure measures should not be interpreted automatically as evidence of achieved outcomes.
Cost reduction and environmental improvement can provide an entry point for integration.
Certification and reporting may remain disconnected from board decisions.
Organisational culture can affect whether measurement becomes embedded in practice.
An identifiable decision owner is important to the practical value of a proposed metric.
Implementation processes can matter as much as the metric formula.
Local decision needs may favour decentralised use within a common framework.
Basic financial and sustainability data may be unavailable before integrated measurement begins.
Linking sustainability activity to profitability may help explain its managerial relevance.
Limited staff capacity can restrict both measurement and experimentation.
Estimation-based sustainability information can be difficult to reconcile with expectations formed in financial accounting.
Aggregation can obscure areas of poor performance.
Returns associated with qualifying capital expenditure were proposed as a possible integrated measure.
